item.title: Berendsen: Netherlands “disapproves” of new Trump ICC sanctions
item.description:
Berendsen: Netherlands “disapproves” of new Trump ICC sanctions

August 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch foreign minister Tom Berendsen has criticised the latest sanctions imposed by the Trump administration against officials of the International Criminal Court, based in The Hague.

Berendsen said international courts “must be able to freely carry out their mandates” after the measures were taken against the court’s president, Tomoko Akane, and senior prosecutor Abdoulaye Saye.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Akane and Saye had been “directly engaged in efforts by the ICC to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute officials whose government ⁠has not consented to ICC jurisdiction.”

Seye was a member of the prosecution team that drafted the arrest warrants against Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the country’s former defence minister Yoav Gallant 18 months ago.

Shortly afterwards Donald Trump issued an executive order authorising sanctions against ICC officials, such as freezing their bank accounts in the US and shutting them out of international payment systems.

The US and Israel are not signatories to the ICC’s founding statutes, but the government of Palestine is. The ICC ruled in 2021 that Gaza and the West Bank fell under its jurisdiction.

Continued support

Berendsen said in a post on social media site X, formerly Twitter: “The Netherlands disapproves of the latest sanctions against officials and staff of the International Criminal Court.”

He went on to offer to meet Akane “to discuss our continued support.” Berendsen did not directly condemn the US government’s actions.

The Netherlands disapproves of the latest sanctions against officials and staff of the International Criminal Court. International courts and tribunals must be able to freely carry out their mandates. 1/2

— Tom Berendsen (@ministerBZ) August 18, 2026


Akane said last year that the sanctions would “rapidly undermine the court’s operations”, while in recent months Rubio has stepped up his rhetoric against the ICC, accusing it of “waging a war against our country” and vowing to dismantle it “brick by brick”.

item.title: Higher oil prices drive up Dutch industrial turnover
item.description:
Higher oil prices drive up Dutch industrial turnover

August 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch industrial turnover rose 8.4% in the second quarter, the biggest year-on-year rise since the end of 2022. But it was driven mainly by higher oil prices rather than a real recovery, figures from national statistics agency CBS show.

Prices across industry were 5% higher than a year ago, so more than half of the rise reflects costlier goods rather than higher sales. Last year, turnover had fallen 0.7%.

The growth was also uneven, with refineries and the chemical industry taking in 31.2% more than a year earlier, and the oil industry alone up 83% as its selling prices rose 40.5%.

The higher oil prices stem from disruption to the Strait of Hormuz, which has been largely shut since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February. With few ships getting through, prices have risen – the same reason petrol has been so expensive in the Netherlands this year.

Not every sector grew. Food, drink and tobacco fell furthest, with turnover down 6.7%, mainly because selling prices dropped. Shoppers are unlikely to see that in the supermarket yet, as there are many steps between factory and shelf.

Manufacturers are more optimistic about the months ahead, with more expecting higher turnover than at any point since mid-2022. Even so, many still cannot find enough workers, and slightly more industrial companies went bankrupt than a year earlier, CBS said.

item.title: “Exceptional” 17th-century sketchbook donated to Rijksmuseum
item.description:
“Exceptional” 17th-century sketchbook donated to Rijksmuseum

August 18, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A 17th-century sketchbook containing 30 drawings has been hailed as a rare find after it was donated to the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.

Several of the sketches have been attributed to the Frisian painter Rombould Uylenburgh, who was a well-known artist in his day but fell into obscurity following his death in 1627 or 1628.

The book is known as the Van Eeghen sketchbook, after the family of Amsterdam merchants who owned it for three centuries. The sketches, some of which were made on blue paper, have retained their colour because the book has not been on display.

The Rijksmuseum said it was unusual for an artist’s sketchbook from the 17th century to survive intact for so long. More commonly, the drawings are torn out and sold individually, or lost.

Only two sketches and a handful of paintings by Uylenburgh were thought to have survived when the sketchbook resurfaced in 1935.

The drawings in the book were only attributed to him in 2013, after the owner saw they were similar to one of the artist’s works in the Rijksmuseum’s collection.

Uylenburgh was born in Friesland in 1580 but spent most of his life in Poland after his family emigrated to Krakow. He because the court painter of King Sigismund III Vasa and went on to build a successful career in the port city of Danzig.

His brother, Hendrik, returned to the Dutch Republic and based himself in Amsterdam. By 1625 had established himself as Rembrandt’s main art dealer and is believed to have introduced the painter to his cousin, Saskia van Uylenburgh, who married Rembrandt in 1633.

The Van Eeghen sketchbook is the focus of a display in the museum from August 19 until November 29.

item.title: Holidaymakers warned not to bring home “destructive” beetle
item.description:
Holidaymakers warned not to bring home “destructive” beetle

August 18, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch food standards watchdog NVWA has urged returning holidaymakers not to bring back foreign invaders after a Japanese beetle was found in a freight shipment from Italy.

The insect was found dead in a plastic container that was being transported from a region of Italy where Japanese beetles are known to live.

The NVWA set traps in the container to see if any live beetles had crept inside, but none were found. But the agency told people coming back from southern Europe and transport companies to be alert and report any specimens they found.

“The NVWA is explicitly asking trading and logistics companies to be alert for beetles hitching a lift when they travel to or through the named areas,” the agency said in a statement.

“Do not in any event leave the doors and windows of your vehicle open for longer than necessary and try to check goods and packing for beetles before departure if possible.“

Japanese beetles are not considered a pest in their native country, where their numbers are controlled by natural predators.

But in recent years they have been spotted in Italy, Croatia, Switzerland, Germany and the Azores. The German province of Hessen is the closest area to the Netherlands with an established population.

They are regarded as highly destructive because they feed on a wide range of vegetation. Adult beetles will devour leaves and stems of plants, while their larvae eat grass roots and weeds.

The NVWA has also published advice on its website advising people how to tell Japanese beetles apart from similar looking native species.

item.title: Inflation making plant-based foods cheaper than meat and dairy
item.description:
Inflation making plant-based foods cheaper than meat and dairy

August 18, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Plant-based foods now cost less than meat and dairy equivalents at nine major supermarkets in the Netherlands, according to new research published by food organisation ProVeg.

“It’s remarkable that this is happening,” Martine van Haperen, nutrition and health expert at ProVeg, told DutchNews.

“It’s normally been very difficult for plant-based products to compete with animal-based ones. What we’re seeing now is that store brands like Albert Heijn have expanded their own-brand products, making them more affordable.”

The bigger driver, she said, is inflation. “Inflation has hit animal products much harder than plant-based ones, and that is because animal products require much more resources to be produced.”

Cheaper across the board
ProVeg, which has tracked the price gap since 2022, compared the cheapest plant-based version of each product with the cheapest animal one, priced per kilo, at nine chains in late April.

A basic basket of six items stocked everywhere – mince, burgers, butter, milk, yoghurt and cheese – was cheaper in its plant-based form at every chain, by around 18% on average.

Shoppers buying staples such as mince and milk can save up to 30%, the organisation said, with the widest gaps at Plus and Dirk and the narrowest at the organic chain Ekoplaza. Plant-based butter came in 48% cheaper.

The plant-based versions of some products remain far more expensive, however: mayonnaise costs almost four times as much as the animal version, while vegan yoghurt and kwark are both more than double the price.

The bigger basket
ProVeg also compared a wider basket of 14 products – adding items such as sausages, shoarma and mayonnaise that not every chain sells in a plant-based version. On that fuller list the plant-based basket costs more at four shops: Dirk, Hoogvliet, Jumbo and Picnic. At Albert Heijn the two come out level.

Dirk is the odd one out, with its plant-based basics are among the cheapest of any chain, but its wider basket ends up 25% more expensive than the meat one. It stocks a plant-based version in all 14 categories – just not a cheap own-brand in every one, and those pricier extras drag the total up.

item.title: Police get stop and search powers after shootings in Zuidoost
item.description:
Police get stop and search powers after shootings in Zuidoost

August 18, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Police will be able to stop and search anyone for weapons in part of Amsterdam-Zuidoost for a week from Thursday, after a long series of shooting and gun threats that the city says often involve minors.

The mayor, police and public prosecutor have designated the H-buurt, the K-buurt and the Nelson Mandelapark a security risk area until August 27. Inside it, police can search people without having any specific cause for suspicion.

Authorities recorded 18 firearm-related incidents in the area between June 1 and August 1, ranging from threats made at gunpoint to shootings that left people wounded.

In one case on August 3, a shot fired during a confrontation passed through a wall into a child’s bedroom. A minor was inside the house at the time, reported local broadcaster AT5.

Second summer running
It is the second summer in a row that Zuidoost has faced such a regime. Last year’s designation followed the fatal shooting of a 17-year-old and was extended into September.

Extra police patrols had already been deployed this summer, the city said, but had not been enough to restore calm.

Controversial tactics
Preventive searching has been used in Rotterdam for a long time. It was introduced there in 2002 and now covers large parts of Rotterdam-Zuid.

The tactic is controversial, with opposition and coalition parties on Rotterdam’s council having accused the city of ethnic profiling. Stop and searches in Rotterdam require at least three police officers at every search to guard against it.

Amsterdam dropped preventive searching in 2015, deeming it ineffective. The city has still used it repeatedly over the past year, in the red light district, over New Year and now twice in Zuidoost.

item.title: Budget talks offer no clear route to majority for Dutch cabinet
item.description:
Budget talks offer no clear route to majority for Dutch cabinet

August 18, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The cabinet has begun talks with opposition parties to try to secure a majority for next month’s annual budget, with prime minister Rob Jetten setting a target of August 28 to secure a deal.

The three-party coalition of D66, VVD and CDA is 10 seats short of a majority in the lower house and holds less than one-third of the seats in the Senate.

Commentators say the choice boils down to two options: either do a deal with the main left-wing party Progressief Nederland (PRO) – which was formed by the merger of PvdA and GroenLinks – or try to forge a majority on the right with JA21. But neither route is straightforward.

PRO leader Jesse Klaver told NRC this week that he supported the cabinet’s plans to invest €2.1 billion extra in defence and €1 billion in education.

But his party wants to force the cabinet to scrap its proposed €6.5 billion cuts to social security and raise the money instead through higher taxes on wealth and corporations.

Klaver said he was prepared to drive a hard bargain on the welfare cuts even though they are not due to be introduced until next year’s budget. His stance is backed up by the trade union movement, which has called a national transport workers’ strike for September 9 to protest against the reforms.

“We won’t let people live with uncertainty about cuts in the future,” Klaver said. “These need to be taken off the table this autumn.

VVD reluctance

The right-wing liberal VVD says the cuts are non-negotiable because they are not prepared to increase borrowing or let the budget deficit exceed the European Union’s 3% limit.

The VVD has been reluctant to negotiate with PRO, which it explicitly ruled out as a coalition partner during last year’s general election campaign and in the negotiations to form the current cabinet at the start of this year.

But the path to a majority on the right is even more complicated. Support from PRO would give the cabinet a healthy majority in the lower house and a near majority in the Senate, where the government needs to find just two more votes from smaller parties.

JA21 has nine seats in the lower house – one fewer than the number needed for a majority – but only two senators. The party wants the cabinet to cut welfare even further and reduce taxes, including the so-called “freedom contribution” proposed by the Christian Democrats (CDA) to fund defence spending.

JA21: “Constructive”

Its leader, Joost Eerdmans, said a video call with Jetten and the two deputy prime ministers, Dilan Yesilgöz of the VVD and Bart van den Brink of the CDA, had been “good and constructive” and further discussions would follow, without disclosing further details.

Geert Wilders’ far-right PVV group and the even more extreme Forum voor Democratie (FVD), which have 25 seats between them, are refusing to lend the cabinet any support.

DNA, the splinter group of former PVV MPs led by Gidi Markuszower, is willing to co-operate with the cabinet, but has not been invited to the negotiating table.

Markuszower has warned he will demand a high price for his party’s support: “People at home are crying out for more money in their pocket, lower costs, more houses, more secuity and less asylum, but the cabinet is failing on all fronts.”

BBB shut out

The farmers’ party BBB has also been left off the guest list for this week’s talks, even though the party has 11 seats in the Senate.

The BBB has been unhappy with the government’s plans to impose more limits on the agriculture sector in order to cut nitrogen pollution, which has triggered a new wave of farmers’ protests over the summer.

The party has been riven by defections in both houses in the last year, particularly the upper house, where five BBB senators have left the party, including two who switched allegiance to its arch-nemesis, the progressive liberal party D66.

Heinen absent

Even more intriguing is the fact that finance minister Eelco Heinen, who will present the budget when parliament reconvenes on September 15, is not attending the first two days of negotiations.

Heinen excused himself on the basis that the focus of the talks was to secure “political commitment” rather than discuss the details of fiscal policy, but Klaver remarked: “I can’t remember a previous time when the finance minister wasn’t there for the budget process.”

The Christian parties ChristenUnie and SGP, as well as the pensioners’ party 50Plus, are also due to meet with ministers on Wednesday.

item.title: Water board call in police after drought inspectors face threats
item.description:
Water board call in police after drought inspectors face threats

August 18, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Water authorities in Noord-Brabant have contacted police after inspectors received threats for checking whether local residents were breaking drought restrictions.

The Brabantse Delta water board, which covers an area centred on Breda stretching from the Maas to the Belgian border, has imposed a ban on taking water from streams and ditches between 9am and 9pm.

Inspectors have been using drones equipped with cameras to monitor fields since the ban was introduced a month ago. But staff who were named in a recent article on news website Omroep Brabant about their work have since ben subjected to threats.

Water board chairman Joris Bengevoord would not go into detail about the threats, but said a criminal complaint had been filed with police so they could investigate.

“It’s very serious and goes way too far,” he told NOS. “It’s not OK that they’re being threatened, which is why I’m speaking out as water board chair.

“We are doing this with the best intentions and I stand behind my staff. They are in the midst of it day after day.”

item.title: Do you know “Lucky”? Police can’t ID foreign man in Amsterdam
item.description:
Do you know “Lucky”? Police can’t ID foreign man in Amsterdam

August 18, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Amsterdam cold case police are appealing for help identifying a man known as “Lucky” who collapsed on the street three years ago after suffering a suspected brain haemorrhage or stroke.

Doctors believe he subsequently developed aphasia, which makes communication nearly impossible. No one has been able to work out who he is or where he came from.

He now lives in a care home in Amsterdam Zuidoost and the only words he still uses are English ones – “nonsense” and “definitely” – which he uses to confirm or deny things. He spoke in an American or Canadian accent, the police say. Beyond that, he cannot talk or communicate at all.

Detectives first began looking into the case in 2023 but every line of inquiry ran into a dead end. The search then passed to the force’s cold case team, where two retired members, named as Ruud and Nel, are now volunteering to find out who he is. Presumably, somewhere his family or friends are looking for him.

A police spokesperson told DutchNews that they have tried to find his identity through DNA databases and with facial recognition technologies, but to no avail. Strict privacy rules limit their powers to access larger data sources where a match could be found, they said.

People who knew him think he may have come from the US or Canada because of his accent. He also may have had a past in Nepal.

A public appeal for information has garnered an “overwhelming” response, police say, with more than 140 tip-offs reported on the first day.

Two nicknames, conflicting clues
Digging into his former social circle, the investigators found that he belonged to a Buddhist community on Middenweg, in the east of the city, where he was known as “Lucky”.

They also learned that he would occasionally have a drink at Soep en Zo, a café on Waterlooplein, where regulars knew him by a different name again: “Chris the Canadian”.

A worker at Soep en Zo who remembers him told DutchNews that he would frequent the shop, often looking shabby and seeming mentally unwell. He always carried a suitcase with him, and would ask for very particular variations of soup, which they would accommodate. He always had money despite his appearance.

Investigators say a lot of the information they’ve gathered is conflicting. “He was supposedly filthy rich, but at the same time he was wandering the streets of Amsterdam,” according to Ruud.

But what the investigators cannot understand is how a person could leave so little trace. “I simply cannot believe that nobody knows who this man really is,” Nel said. “Isn’t it strange that you could perhaps live under the radar in the Netherlands for 20 years?”

“Every person has the right to an identity,” Ruud stressed, “and that includes this man.”

Anyone with potential information on the case can report it to the police here.

item.title: Campaigners call for Amsterdam to pull plug on giant data centre
item.description:
Campaigners call for Amsterdam to pull plug on giant data centre

August 18, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

More than 500 people have joined a campaign to stop a huge data centre being built in Amsterdam-Zuid, arguing that it will bring “zero benefits to the area”.

The Dutch government has introduced restrictions on the size of data centres in recent years following criticism from provincial and municipal governments about the strain on the electricity network. Data centres accounted for 4.6% of all electricity use in the Netherlands in 2024.

But the plans to build a 24,000 m2 facility on Amsterdam’s Science Park were submitted by US firm Equinix before the ban, which only applies to new developments, took effect in 2022.

Local residents have also become increasingly vocal in opposing the construction of data centres, while campaign groups Geef Tegengas and Extinction Rebellion both staged demonstrations this summer against a Microsoft project in Amsterdam Sloterdijk.

“There are already enough data centres to keep everything running. This is becoming overkill,” Dylan Bakker of Stop Datacenter Zuidoost told NOS.

Amsterdam city council, which wants to build 8,000 homes in Zuidoost to help relieve the national housing shortage, has attached extra conditions to the site, such as requiring the residual heat from the plant to be used for domestic heating.

Water and electricity

There are also concerns about the strain on water supplies, which have been exacerbated by the summer drought. Equinix said in its planning application that it would need 274 million litres of water a year for the first stage of the project, rising to more than a billion litres when the data centre is complete in 2036.

But the municipality says it would face legal action and penalties if it tore up the permit to build the data center at this stage.

Equinix has said it will only build one of four planned 60-metre data towers initially, until electricity grid operator Tennet can supply enough power.

Tennet warned earlier this year that the network was nearing capacity, leading to a six-month moratorium on new connections in Utrecht.

The complete campus in Zuidoost will consume 779 kWh of electricity a year, almost as much as all the households Amsterdam combined, which currently use 869 kWh.

Michiel Eielts, director of Equinix Benelux, argued that the data centres were an essential part of modern infrastructure. “Every house needs the internet. We need data centres for the growth of our companies, our public services and our security,” he said.
